title: IRR: Internal Rate of Return
subtitle: The discount rate that makes NPV = 0 - measuring a project's true return
openingOptions: No - the IRR is too high
Yes - IRR > WACC means the project earns more than the cost of capital
explanation: IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0. When IRR > WACC (or the hurdle rate), the project earns more than its cost of capital → invest. IRR < WACC → reject. In this example, an IRR of 15% above a WACC of 10% means the project generates a return 5 percentage points above the cost of raising capital.

realWorldExample.description: Infrastructure projects (seaports, airports, energy) are usually evaluated using both NPV and IRR - IRR communicates an easy-to-grasp 'percentage return' to management and investors, while NPV shows exactly how much absolute value is created.

quiz.question: What is IRR's biggest weakness compared to NPV?
options: IRR does not account for the time value of cash flows
It assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself, which is often unrealistic
IRR only works for projects with a lifespan under five years
IRR requires knowing the cost of capital in advance before it can even be calculated at all
quiz.explanation: IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR - if IRR = 40%, this assumption isn't realistic. Also, with cash flows that change sign multiple times, there can be multiple IRRs. NPV doesn't have these problems.

quiz.question: Two projects both have an IRR of 20%, but project A is 100 billion in scale while B is 10 billion. If the company can only choose one, is an equal IRR enough to conclude the two projects create equal value?
options: Yes, but only if both projects have the same payback period
Yes, because an equal IRR means equal efficiency in using capital
No, because IRR measures a percentage, not value
No, because a smaller project always carries more risk than a larger one
quiz.explanation: This is a classic IRR limitation: it measures the return as a PERCENTAGE, not absolute value. A project with a high IRR but small scale can create less absolute value than a project with a slightly lower IRR but much larger scale - this is why NPV is usually preferred when choosing between mutually exclusive projects.

quiz.question: What exactly is IRR defined as?
options: The minimum return the investment committee requires
The average annual profit rate of the project
The ratio of total cash received over the project's life to the initial investment amount
The discount rate that makes the project's NPV exactly zero
quiz.explanation: IRR is the root of the equation NPV = 0. It is not a return the firm sets as a target - that's the hurdle rate, and comparing IRR to the hurdle rate is what drives the decision.

quiz.question: A project has an IRR of 14%, WACC of 11%. What should be done?
options: Proceed, because the project's return exceeds the cost of capital
Don't proceed, because the margin is too thin
Proceed only if the payback period is under three years and cash flow is guaranteed
Can't decide without knowing the project's scale
quiz.explanation: IRR > WACC means the project earns more than what it costs to raise the capital, equivalent to a positive NPV. Three percentage points is a thin margin so it's worth running more scenarios, but the initial signal is to proceed.

quiz.question: When can a project have more than one IRR value?
options: When the project runs over ten years with rising cash flows
When the cash flow changes sign more than once over the project's life
When a company uses multiple funding sources, each carrying a different cost of capital
When the first year's cash flow exceeds the initial investment
quiz.explanation: The equation NPV = 0 is a polynomial, so the number of roots depends on the number of sign changes in the cash flow. A mine that must spend heavily on remediation at the end of its life is a classic example - and in that case, IRR loses its meaning; only NPV remains usable.

keyTakeaways: IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0
Weakness: the unrealistic reinvestment assumption; multiple IRRs are possible

practicePrompt.question: A project has a positive NPV at a discount rate of 10%, but when the discount rate is raised to 18%, the NPV becomes exactly zero. What is this 18% figure called, and what does it mean for investment decision-making?
options: The 18% is the IRR - the discount rate at which the project's NPV comes out at zero
18% is a random number with no particular significance in analyzing the investment project
18% is the guaranteed rate of return the company will definitely receive from this project every year
18% is the minimum discount rate legally mandated for all investment projects
practicePrompt.explanation: IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0 - this is the project's 'breakeven rate of return'. If the company's actual cost of capital (hurdle rate) is lower than the IRR, the project creates positive value; if higher than the IRR, the project destroys value - this is why IRR is used alongside NPV to evaluate investment projects.

summary.keyIdea: IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Find IRR by trial and error
application.message: Using the same cash flow you used in the NPV lesson, try a few different discount rates until NPV is close to zero - that's the project's estimated IRR.
application.secondary: You don't need perfect precision, the goal is to get a feel for how IRR behaves.

sections.text: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) answers the question: what percentage return does this project actually earn each year? Mathematically, IRR is exactly the discount rate that makes a project's NPV equal to zero.

Instead of being given a discount rate to compute NPV, IRR works backward to find the discount rate that makes NPV = 0. Decision rule: if IRR > WACC (or the hurdle rate the company sets), the project earns more than the cost of capital → invest. If IRR < WACC, the project doesn't cover the cost of capital → reject. IRR is popular because it's easy to communicate: saying 'this project has an IRR of 18%' is much easier to grasp than 'the project's NPV is 258 million VND'.

IRR implicitly assumes that all intermediate cash flows are reinvested at that same IRR - if the IRR comes out to 40%, this assumption is almost unrealistic because it's very hard to find continuous reinvestment opportunities at that high a return. In addition, if a project's cash flow changes sign multiple times (e.g., negative - positive - negative), the equation NPV = 0 can have multiple roots, producing several different IRRs at once - rendering the metric meaningless.

sections.title: IRR is the root of an equation, not a direct calculation

variables.name: The unknown to solve for
variables.description: There's no closed-form solution once the project runs longer than two periods. Excel and financial calculators solve it by iteration, which is why the IRR function sometimes throws an error when it fails to converge.

variables.name: Cash flow in year t
variables.description: The exact cash flow used to compute NPV. Same numbers, different question: NPV is given r to find the value, IRR is given value = 0 to find r.

example.title: The same three-year project as before
example.calculation: Outlay 500, receive 200 each year for 3 years. Try r = 9%: NPV = +6.3. Try r = 10%: NPV = −2.6. The root lies between these two.
example.explanation: Cost of capital 10% > IRR 9.7% so reject - the same conclusion NPV already gave with a negative value. The two measures always agree on whether to accept or reject A SINGLE project; they only clash when RANKING multiple projects.

sections.text: Where IRR lies: the reinvestment assumption

When the calculator outputs an IRR of 40%, that figure is only accurate if every dollar the project pays out along the way is reinvested at exactly 40%. In real life, the cash coming back from a project usually just sits in an account or pays down debt - earning a return around the cost of capital, not around the IRR. So the higher the IRR, the more inflated it becomes, and a project with a 40% IRR rarely actually doubles wealth as fast as that number promises. NPV doesn't have this problem because it discounts everything at the same r - exactly the rate the money actually earns.

sections.label: Multiple IRRs at once - when and why
sections.text: A mine: spend 100 to open it, receive 300 during operation, then spend 250 more on remediation when it closes. The cash flow changes sign twice, so the NPV = 0 equation is quadratic and has two roots - both 10% and 150% are 'the IRR'. Neither is meaningful. A rough but usable rule: however many times a cash flow changes sign, that's how many IRRs there might be. When that happens, drop IRR and use NPV instead.

left.label: When they agree
left.text: A standalone project with a cash flow that changes sign exactly once: IRR > r is always equivalent to NPV > 0. Either measure gives the same decision.

right.label: When they clash
right.text: Two mutually exclusive projects, differing in scale or in the shape of their cash flows over time. Then NPV wins the argument: it measures how much richer shareholders get, while IRR only measures speed.

items: IRR > WACC: accept the project; IRR < WACC: reject
Between mutually exclusive projects, an equal IRR does not mean equal value created - the larger-scale project usually creates a larger absolute NPV
Cash flows that change sign multiple times can produce multiple IRRs - use NPV instead in that case
NPV is generally preferred over IRR whenever the two metrics disagree on ranking projects

lines: IRR answers 'what percentage return', but when you need to know 'how much money is created', NPV is always the more reliable answer.
Both ignore a question many executives ask first: how long until the capital comes back? The next lesson covers that measure, and why it's dangerous to use on its own.
